clinicalPearls: A rare osteochondrosis affecting the epiphyses of the phalanges of the hands (and sometimes toes)
It typically presents in adolescence with painless or mildly painful swelling of the interphalangeal joints
There may be a familial (autosomal dominant) pattern in some cases
Radiographs show irregularity, fragmentation and flattening of the phalangeal epiphyses
It can be mistaken for juvenile inflammatory arthritis, but inflammatory markers are normal and there is no true synovitis
The course is usually benign, though residual joint deformity or early osteoarthritis may occur
reference.pathophysiology: Thiemann disease is an osteochondrosis in which the epiphyses of the phalanges undergo avascular change with disturbed endochondral ossification during growth. The affected epiphyses become fragmented and flattened before reconstituting, and the process is thought to reflect ischaemia of the growing epiphysis, sometimes with a hereditary predisposition. The result is enlargement and deformity of the interphalangeal joints, which can lead to residual deformity or secondary degenerative change.
additionalInvestigations: Radiographs of the hands showing epiphyseal changes
Inflammatory markers and autoantibodies (normal, to exclude arthritis)
Family history and, where relevant, assessment for a hereditary pattern
Clinical assessment of the interphalangeal joints
Exclusion of skeletal dysplasia if widespread
redFlags: Widespread epiphyseal disease suggesting a dysplasia
reference.prognosis: The condition is generally benign and self-limiting with skeletal maturity, although some patients are left with digital deformity or early interphalangeal osteoarthritis.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing it as juvenile idiopathic arthritis and giving unnecessary treatment
Attributing normal-marker joint swelling to inflammation
management: Reassurance and conservative management are the mainstay, as the osteochondrosis is generally benign and self-limiting at skeletal maturity
Provide symptomatic relief with simple analgesia or anti-inflammatories, activity modification and splinting during painful phases
Confirm normal inflammatory markers and autoantibodies to distinguish it from juvenile inflammatory arthritis and avoid unnecessary immunosuppression
Offer hand therapy and physiotherapy to maintain interphalangeal joint function
Monitor radiographically for residual digital deformity or early interphalangeal osteoarthritis
Refer to orthopaedics for persistent deformity, and consider genetic counselling where an autosomal dominant familial pattern is evident
